result.summary: Rome is struck by plague, and the Delphic oracle tells the Romans to fetch Apollo's son Æsculapius from Epidaurus. The god appears in a dream and then as a serpent, sails to Rome, and settles on the Tiber island, ending the plague.

scenes.title: Plague and the Delphic oracle
scenes.summary: Plague ravages Latium and the Romans consult Phœbus at Delphi. The tripod tells them to seek his son, and the Senate sends envoys to Epidaurus.
scenes.stakes: The Romans face death from the plague unless they obey the oracle and find a cure.

scenes.title: Debate and the dream at Epidaurus
scenes.summary: The Epidaurian elders are divided about giving up their god. Æsculapius appears to a Roman in a dream and shows the serpent he will become.
scenes.stakes: Epidaurus risks losing its protector, and Rome's envoys risk returning without the god.

scenes.title: The serpent god boards the ship
scenes.summary: At dawn the nobles pray, and the god appears as a great serpent. He is acknowledged by the priest, leaves his temple, and boards the Roman ship.
scenes.stakes: Rome's hope of cure depends on the god consenting to depart.

scenes.title: Voyage along the Italian coast
scenes.summary: The ship sails across the Ionian sea and up the Italian coast. The god visits his father's temple at Antium before continuing.
scenes.stakes: The voyage could be lost to rough sea.

place.name: Ionian Sea and coast of Italy

scenes.title: Arrival at Rome and the Island
scenes.summary: Crowds welcome the god at the Tiber. He chooses the river island, resumes his divine form, and ends the mourning.

alias_notes.explanation: Ausonian and Latian are poetic names for Italian or Roman.

notable_quotes.reason: The oracle says Rome needs not Apollo but Apollo's son.
Closing line: the healing god arrives in Rome.

analysis.text: This episode links Greek myth to Roman history, showing a foreign god adopted by Rome. It leads towards the Julius Caesar and Augustus finale.
It recalls the real introduction of Aesculapius's cult to Rome around 293 BC during a plague, with a temple on Tiber Island.

legacy.text: The Tiber island long held a sanctuary of healing, and a hospital still stands there.

fun_facts.text: The Tiber island was said to be shaped like a ship, and its edges were later carved with a ship design.

language_notes.text: The Island in the Tiber is Tiber Island in Rome, where Æsculapius's temple stood. The Romans associated its shape with the ship that brought the god.
Delphi was regarded as the centre of the world, the 'navel' (omphalos), where Zeus's two eagles were said to have met.
Tripod: the three-legged seat on which the priestess (Pythia) sat to deliver Apollo's oracles.
Epidaurus: a Greek city in the Argolid, the chief cult centre of Æsculapius, famous as a healing sanctuary.
Ausonian: poetic name for Italian, from the Ausones, an early people of Italy.
The god promises a size fit for a transformed heavenly body, probably alluding to the deification of the dead, such as Caesar's transformation into a star.
"The God sought" means the god they had come to seek: Aesculapius, whose temple at Epidaurus they visit.
A fillet is a band or ribbon worn around the head, here marking the priest's ritual purity.
"Be of good omen" means to speak and think only auspicious things, as Roman ritual required, so that nothing disrupts the rite.
The "descendants of Æneas" are the Romans, who traced their origin to the Trojan hero Æneas.
Ausonian means Italian; Ausonia was a poetic name for Italy, so this is the Roman ship.
The bull is a sacrificial offering to secure a safe voyage, made before the ship's cables are loosed.
"The daughter of Pallas" is Aurora, the dawn; "the sixth rising" means the sixth dawn of the voyage.
"The king the grandson of Hippotas" is Aeolus, ruler of the winds, whose island lay near the Sicilian strait.
"She for whom her foster-child erected the tomb" is Caieta, nurse of Aeneas, who gave her name to Caieta (Gaeta).
"The God of Epidaurus" is Aesculapius in serpent form; "his sire" is Phoebus (Apollo), whose temple stood at Antium.
"Son of Phœbus" is Aesculapius; "Latian" means Latin, i.e. Roman.

context_notes.text: Phœbus Apollo was god of prophecy and healing. Æsculapius, his son by Coronis, was the god of medicine.
Æsculapius is conventionally shown bearded, leaning on a staff with a serpent coiled around it, as the dream describes.
The serpent was the sacred animal of Aesculapius, god of healing, whom the Romans are bringing to Rome to end a plague.
The harbour is that of Epidaurus, the Greek city where Aesculapius had his famous temple.
Vesta was the goddess of the hearth; her priestesses, the Vestal Virgins, kept her sacred fire burning in Rome.
This is the Tiber Island in Rome, where a temple of Aesculapius was built after the plague of 291 BC.

literary_notes.text: The narrator addresses the Muses directly, invoking them as sources of knowledge, a traditional epic gesture that renews the poem's authority.
The place, laurels and quivers shake together, as if the sanctuary itself reacts to the god's presence.
The narrator suddenly addresses the sleeping Roman as 'thou', making the dream vivid and immediate.
Repeating 'departs' for the god and then for sleep links the two departures and gives a smooth, quiet close.
Gold glitter, fiery eyes and the shaking temple give a vivid sense of divine power and awe.
The god's backward look at his old altars humanizes him, giving his departure a tender, reluctant tone.
The ship "is sensible of" the god's weight, as if it could feel the divinity it carries.
The narrator breaks off to address Vesta directly, giving the welcome a ceremonial, reverent tone.
Calling Rome "the sovereign of the world" marks the city's imperial greatness and flatters Ovid's Roman audience.
The serpent's return to divine form quietly resolves the story's transformation and ends the city's grief.
